source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως σφόδρα εὔηθες λέγει ὅτι, εἴπερ ἀτόπους ἀπολογίας εὑρίσκοντες, ἐφ᾿ αἷς καταγελάστως ἐξηπατήθητε, οἴεσθε ἀληθῶς ἀπολογεῖσθαι, τί κωλύει καὶ ἄλλους, ὅσοι καταγνωσθέντες κακοδαιμονέστερον ἀπήλλαξαν, μείζονας νομίζειν εἶναι καὶ θειοτέρους τούτους ἀγγέλους; ὅτι δ᾿ ἄντικρυς καὶ σαφῶς οὐδὲν ὅμοιον ἔχει ὁ παθὼν τὰ ἀναγεγραμμένα Ἰησοῦς τοῖς κακοδαιμονέστερον ἀπαλλάξασι διὰ γοητείαν ἢ ὁτιδήποτε ἔγκλημα ἄλλο, παντί τῳ δῆλον. οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναταί τις παραστῆσαι γοήτων ἔργον ἐπιστρέψαν ψυχὰς ἀπὸ τῶν πολλῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἁμαρτημάτων καὶ τῆς κατὰ τὴν κακίαν χύσεως. ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ λῃσταῖς αὐτὸν παραβαλὼν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖός φησιν ὅτι δύναιτο ἄν τις ὁμοίως ἀναισχυντῶν καὶ περὶ λῃστοῦ καὶ ἀνδροφόνου κολασθέντος εἰπεῖν ὅτι οὗτός γε οὐχὶ λῃστὴς ἀλλὰ θεὸς ἦν· προεῖπε γὰρ τοῖς συλλῄσταις ὅτι πείσεται τοιαῦτα, οἷα δὴ πέπονθε· λέγοιτ᾿ ἂν πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι οὐ παρὰ τὸ προειρηκέναι αὐτὸν ταῦτα πείσεσθαι τοιαῦτα ὑπολαμβάνομεν περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ὁποῖα καὶ φρονοῦντες παῤῥησιαζόμεθα ἐν αὐτῷ ὡς ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἡμῖν κατεληλυθότι· δεύτερον δὲ καὶ ταῦτα λέγομεν ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις προειρῆσθαί πως, ἐπεὶ „μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη“ ὁ θεὸς παρὰ τοῖς ἀνόμοις, λῃστὴν μᾶλλον τὸν „διὰ στάσιν“ „καὶ φόνον“ βληθέντα εἰς φυλακὴν βουλομένοις ἀπολυθῆναι τὸν δ᾿ Ἰησοῦν σταυρῶσαι, καὶ σταυρώσασιν αὐτὸν μεταξὺ λῃστῶν δύο. καὶ ἀεὶ δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς γνησίοις μαθηταῖς καὶ μαρτυροῦσι τῇ ἀληθείᾳ ὁ Ἰησοῦς συσταυροῦται λῃσταῖς καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν αὐτοῖς παρὰ ἀνθρώποις καταδίκην πάσχει. καί φαμεν ὅτι, εἴπερ οὗτοι ὅμοιόν τι λῃσταῖς ἔχουσιν οἱ διὰ τὴν εἰς τὸν δημιουργὸν εὐσέβειαν, ἵνα αὐτὴν εἰλικρινῆ καὶ καθαρὰν διαφυλάξωσι κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίαν, πᾶσαν αἰκίαν καὶ πάντας θανάτους ἀναδεχόμενοι, δῆλον ὅτι καὶ ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ὁ πατὴρ τῆς τοιαύτης διδασκαλίας, εὐλόγως ὑπὸ τοῦ Κέλσου λῃστάρχαις παραβάλλεται. ἀλλ᾿ οὔτ᾿ ἐκεῖνος κατὰ τὸ κοινωνικὸν ἀποθνῄσκων οὔθ᾿ οὗτοι δι᾿ εὐσέβειαν ταῦτα πάσχοντες καὶ μόνοι πάντων ἀνθρώπων διὰ τὴν φανεῖσαν αὐτοῖς ὁδὸν τῆς εἰς τὸ θεῖον τιμῆς ἐπιβουλευόμενοι οὐκ ἀδίκως ἀναιροῦνται, οὔθ᾿ ὁ Ἰησοῦς οὐκ ἀσεβῶς ἐπεβουλεύθη.
pass_a_gloss: Next to these, I do not know how, he says [something] very silly (εὔηθες): that, if finding absurd (ἄτοπος) defences (ἀπολογία), over/by which you were laughably (καταγελάστως) deceived (ἐξαπατάω), you think you truly defend yourselves (ἀπολογέομαι), what prevents (κωλύω) also [you thinking] others, as many as having been condemned (καταγιγνώσκω) departed (ἀπαλλάσσω) more wretchedly (κακοδαιμονέστερον), to be greater and more divine (θειότερος) - these - messengers/angels (ἄγγελοι)? But that plainly (ἄντικρυς) and clearly (σαφῶς) Jesus who suffered the recorded things has nothing like those who departed more wretchedly through sorcery (γοητεία) or any other charge (ἔγκλημα) whatever, is clear to anyone. For no one can present a work of sorcerers (γόης) having turned (ἐπιστρέφω) souls from the many sins (ἁμάρτημα) among men and the outpouring/dissoluteness (χύσις) in vice (κακία). And since, comparing (παραβάλλω) him also to robbers (λῃσταί), the Jew in Celsus says that one could similarly being shameless (ἀναισχυντέω) say also of a robber and murderer (ἀνδροφόνος) punished (κολάζω) that this one was no robber but a god (θεός); for he foretold to his fellow-robbers (συλλῃσταί) that he would suffer such things as indeed he suffered: it might be said first that not on account of his having foretold that he would suffer such things do we suppose (ὑπολαμβάνω) such things about Jesus as, also thinking (φρονέω), we speak boldly (παρρησιάζομαι) concerning him as having come down (κατέρχομαι) to us from God; second we say also these things to have been foretold in a way (πως) in the Gospels, since "with lawless ones (ἄνομοι) he was reckoned (λογίζομαι)" - God among/by the lawless, [they] wishing rather a robber, the one thrown (βάλλω) into prison (φυλακή) "through sedition (στάσις)" "and murder (φόνος)", to be released (ἀπολύω) and Jesus to crucify (σταυρόω), and having crucified him between two robbers. And always in the genuine (γνήσιος) disciples and those bearing witness (μαρτυρέω) to the truth Jesus is crucified with (συσταυρόομαι) robbers and suffers the same condemnation (καταδίκη) as they among men. And we say that, if these have something like robbers, who on account of piety (εὐσέβεια) toward the Creator (δημιουργός), in order that they may preserve (διαφυλάσσω) it sincere (εἰλικρινής) and pure according to the teaching of Jesus, accept (ἀναδέχομαι) every outrage (αἰκία) and all deaths, it is clear that Jesus too, the father of such teaching, is reasonably (εὐλόγως) compared by Celsus to robber-chiefs (λῄσταρχοι). But neither that one dying for the common good (κατὰ τὸ κοινωνικόν), nor these suffering these things for piety and alone of all men plotted against (ἐπιβουλεύω) through the way (ὁδός) that has appeared (φαίνομαι) to them of honour (τιμή) toward the divine (τὸ θεῖον), are not-unjustly (οὐκ ἀδίκως) killed (ἀναιρέω), nor was Jesus not-impiously (οὐκ ἀσεβῶς) plotted against.
pass_b_english: Next, somehow or other, he says something very silly: “If, when you come up with absurd defences by which you have been ridiculously deceived, you think that you are truly making a defence, what prevents you from thinking that others as well, all who have been condemned and come to a more miserable end, are greater and more divine messengers than he?” But it is plain to anyone that Jesus, who suffered what is recorded, is openly and clearly unlike those who came to a more miserable end because of sorcery or any other charge whatever. For no one can point to a work of sorcerers that has turned souls from the many sins found among men and from the flood of vice.

And since the Jew in Celsus also compares him to robbers and says: “One could, with like shamelessness, say also of a robber and murderer who had been punished that this man was no robber but a god, for he foretold to his fellow robbers that he would suffer such things as he did suffer,” it might be said, first, that it is not because he foretold that he would suffer such things that we think of Jesus as we do, and boldly declare it of him as one who has come down to us from God. Second, we say that even these things were in some way foretold in the Gospels, since God “was numbered with the lawless” (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12) in the judgment of lawless men, who wanted rather a robber released, the one who had been thrown into prison “for sedition” “and murder” (Luke 23:18–19; John 18:40), and Jesus crucified, and who crucified him between two robbers (Matthew 27:38).

And in his genuine disciples, who bear witness to the truth, Jesus is always crucified with robbers and suffers among men the same condemnation as they do. And we say that if these men, who for the sake of their piety toward the Creator accept every outrage and every kind of death so as to keep that piety sincere and pure according to the teaching of Jesus, are in any way like robbers, then it is clear that Jesus also, the father of such teaching, is reasonably compared by Celsus to robber chiefs. But neither he, who died for the common good, nor these, who suffer such things for piety and alone of all men are plotted against because of the way of honouring the divine that has been shown to them, are put to death justly; nor was the plot against Jesus anything but impious.

notes: Translated from the Greek of the staged Koetschau row only; Crombie (ANF) and Chadwick were not used.
Independent clause review: every clause checked; verdict pass.
Scripture citations sit inline beside the clause in Pass B.
2.44: Koetschau prints ὁ θεός ('God was numbered with the lawless'). This is kept as printed and noted as possibly corrupt. Worth an owner check against the apparatus if one is available.
2.44: 'than he' is supplied for the awkward τούτους ἀγγέλους, as already noted by the translator. Left as is.

translator_notes: Two quotations of Celsus are kept in quotation marks: the general objection (introduced by λέγει ὅτι) and the words of “the Jew in Celsus” about the robber. In the first, the transmitted τούτους ἀγγέλους is awkward; it is taken as resumptive (“others ... these”), and “than he” is supplied from the context of the comparison with Jesus; a reading τούτου (“than this man”) would give the same sense. ἄγγελοι is rendered “messengers” (Celsus’s sneer at Christians calling Jesus a messenger from God); “angels” is the other possible sense. ὑπολαμβάνομεν ... τοιαῦτα ... ὁποῖα καὶ φρονοῦντες παρρησιαζόμεθα ἐν αὐτῷ is rendered “we think of Jesus as we do, and boldly declare it of him”, to avoid a doubled “hold”. “Numbered with the lawless” (μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη) matches Luke 22:37 exactly, where Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12 (LXX ἐν τοῖς ἀνόμοις ἐλογίσθη; same chapter and verse in English Bibles); Origen says “in the Gospels”, so Luke is cited first. The transmitted ὁ θεὸς (“God was numbered”) is kept as printed by Koetschau, though it is unusual and may be corrupt. “For sedition and murder ... thrown into prison” matches Luke 23:19 (διὰ στάσιν ... καὶ φόνον βληθεὶς ἐν τῇ φυλακῇ); that Barabbas was a robber is John 18:40; two robbers crucified with him is Matthew 27:38. The closing sentence has a compound negative followed by simple negatives (οὔτ᾿ ... οὔθ᾿ ... οὐκ ἀδίκως ... οὔθ᾿ ... οὐκ ἀσεβῶς); a simple negative after a compound one keeps its own force, so the sense is that they are killed unjustly and the plot against Jesus was impious, and the English states this plainly. ἐκεῖνος ... κατὰ τὸ κοινωνικὸν ἀποθνῄσκων is taken of Jesus, who died for the common good of mankind; the later “nor was Jesus” then restates the point. χύσις (“outpouring, dissoluteness”) is rendered “flood of vice”.
